messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: QA Engineer
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 46

# Vignette: Ernesto, Age 75

Ernesto has spent the better part of five decades making sure things don't fall apart. As a QA engineer, his entire professional identity has been built around anticipating failure — reading systems carefully, catching the flaw before it becomes a catastrophe. It is a cruel irony, then, that the event that broke something inside him was one no checklist could have prevented.

Three years ago, a major earthquake struck the region of Colombia where Ernesto had returned to visit extended family. He and his wife, Claudia, were staying in the home of his elderly aunt when the ground began to move at just past two in the morning. The shaking lasted under a minute, but in that time the back wall of the house collapsed, a neighbor's home across the street pancaked entirely, and Ernesto found himself pinned under a fallen ceiling beam in complete darkness, calling out to Claudia and hearing nothing back for what felt like an hour. She was eventually found uninjured in a doorway, following the instructions they had been given years ago. He had not remembered to do the same. He had simply frozen.

Ernesto was physically unharmed, aside from bruising across his shoulder and back. He flew home to the United States within a week, returned to his part-time consulting work, and told almost no one what had happened. He described the earthquake to colleagues as "a close call" and moved on — or tried to.

Within a month, the sleep problems began. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart pounding, the darkness of the bedroom briefly indistinguishable from the darkness under that beam. He does not always remember a dream, but the dread is physical and immediate, and he often cannot return to sleep. He has taken to leaving a lamp on in the hallway, something Claudia has accepted without much comment, though he has never fully explained it to her.

During the day, Ernesto is watchful in ways that exhaust him. He scans the structure of buildings when he enters them — noting ceiling materials, proximity to load-bearing walls, the distance to exits. At family gatherings, he positions himself near doorways. He is aware this behavior is excessive. Knowing that does not stop it. His engineering mind catalogs threats with the same systematic attention he once gave to product defects, except now the system being audited is every room he walks into.

He has become quieter with Claudia and with their adult children. He describes a persistent sense of flatness — that the warmth he used to feel at Sunday dinners or during calls with his grandchildren is somehow muted, as though received through glass. He still shows up. He still participates. But he notices the distance between himself and the moment, and it troubles him.

What troubles him most, he says, is the freezing. In his professional life, Ernesto has always been the person who stays calm and methodical when others panic. He has built a reputation on it. But when the ceiling came down, he did not move toward Claudia. He did not move at all. He returns to those seconds regularly — not in a way that feels like reflection, but in a way that feels like being pulled back against his will, replaying the moment he believes he failed the most basic test of who he is.

He has mentioned the earthquake to his primary care physician only in passing and has not framed what he is experiencing as something requiring attention. He came to his current sessions at Claudia's insistence, after she noticed him gripping the doorframe one evening during a minor tremor from a distant minor quake. He sat with his eyes closed for several minutes afterward and could not explain to her what was happening inside him. He is not sure, even now, that he fully can.
